title: Naked illuminates Kyoto’s cultural traditions in Nijo Castle’s latest digital art spectacular
description: Featuring night-lit gardens, imperial poetry, and custom digital garments. content:
Featuring night-lit gardens, imperial poetry, and custom digital garments.

Kyoto is home to an abundance of heritage fused with modernity: a place where you could espy a traditional building from afar only to discover a familiar mermaid emblazoned on the sign when you draw closer. Tokyo-based creative collective Naked, Inc., known for combining cinematic storytelling with cutting-edge technology, embraces this dichotomy wholeheartedly, having run several digital art exhibitions over the years in some of Japan’s most iconic landmarks, including Himeji Castle and Matsushima. Running from October 23 through December 5, the immersive art exhibition Naked Meets Nijo Castle 2026 once again transforms the castle grounds into a glowing canvas of light, sound, and interactive digital art.

Originally built in 1603 as the Kyoto residence of the Tokugawa shogun, Nijo Castle is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site famed for its stunning traditional architecture and spacious gardens. The 2026 exhibition celebrates the 400th anniversary of the 1626 Kanei Gyoko (Imperial Visit), a momentous five-day event when Emperor Go-Mizunoo visited the castle, sparking a cultural exchange between the imperial court and the samurai elite, with cultural aspects like tea ceremony and flower arrangement blossoming. The shogunate used the event as a chance to legitimize their de facto rule over the now-unified country, whereas the emperor took the opportunity to show the country that the imperial family was still relevant in the current period.

To bring this historic era to life, Naked, Inc. draws inspiration from Tokugawa Masako, the daughter of the shogun and empress consort to Emperor Go-Mizunoo. A central figure of the Kanei era (1624-1645), Masako bridged courtly elegance and samurai culture, leaving a lasting influence on Japanese aesthetic traditions, including the delicate art of the kimono.

As a collaboration with the larger Kanei Gyoko 400th Anniversary Festival, with events being held both within Kyoto and nationwide, visitors to Naked meets Nijo Castle 2026 will encounter a total of three curated zones to enjoy. The journey begins at the grand Karamon Gate (a grand Chinese-style gate featuring intricate wood carvings), illuminated with vivid digital projections displaying class Kanei-era patterns and colors.

As you wander past the Ninomaru Palace, inner moat, and Seiryuen Garden, light and sound installations weave together waka poetry composed by Masako, traditional gosho-zome (imperial court dyeing techniques), and illuminated garden scenery.

In the kitchen forecourt, guests can participate in interactive art, selecting classic design patterns to project directly onto a white kosode (a traditional short-sleeved garment that served as the predecessor to the modern kimono) to wear as digital fashion. Guests can also enjoy Masako’s Night Tea Party, combining art, atmosphere, and traditional tea culture.

The exhibition takes place daily from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., with admission nightly until 9:00 p.m. Advance tickets are available at major Japanese convenience stores and travel companies Jalan and Rakuten Travel (all links below), until October 22 starting at 1,600 yen for weekdays and 2,000 yen for weekends, but standard tickets are 2,000 yen for Mondays to Thursdays and 2,400 yen for weekends and holidays. If you are fortunate to be a student or Kyoto resident, a cashback of 500 yen is offered at the on-site booth with a valid ID.

For anyone eager to experience Kyoto’s cultural heritage through a modern lens, this event promises an unforgettable autumn evening, but for those looking to get more hands on, Naked also recently opened a traditional craft workshop at Kyoto Station.

title: JAL first class cakes can be bought for a bargain, but are they as bougie as they seem?
description: In Japan, a cake that’s “imperfect” can sometimes be perfect. Whenever we’re not eating sweets, you can find us on the Internet, searching for sweets, and the rarer they are, the better. So when our reporter Natsuki Gojo discovered an odd-looking pack of cakes online, she immediately stopped browsing, and when she leaned in and […]
content:
In Japan, a cake that’s “imperfect” can sometimes be perfect.

Whenever we’re not eating sweets, you can find us on the Internet, searching for sweets, and the rarer they are, the better. So when our reporter Natsuki Gojo discovered an odd-looking pack of cakes online, she immediately stopped browsing, and when she leaned in and discovered that it was a kilo (2.2 pounds) of cake ends from the cakes served to Japan Airlines’ first-class passengers, she wasted no time in clicking the purchase button.

Marked as “wake ari” (“imperfect”), Urokoya Sohonten’s “Premium Cake Ends” are inherently imperfect – as off-cuts from the manufacturing process, they would usually be discarded rather than presented for serving. The taste is the same as the more beautiful bits in between the ends, though, and given that they’re made by a long-established confectionery shop founded in 1684, Natsuki was far more interested in the flavour than the presentation.

Still, when they arrived on her doorstep, the cake ends looked beautiful to her eye, with two packs containing four neat towers, and each pack weighing around 500 grams.

Though she’d thought that “cake ends” might turn out to be small bits and leftover scraps, these were far bigger than she imagined, and looked like cakes in their own right.

▼ Comparing the size with a Sylvanian Families baby, and a human hand, gives you an idea of just how big these cakes are.


▼ Plenty of thickness in both the sponge and fresh cream.

She was surprised by how hefty they were too, because when she went to take a selfie with them, she found they were difficult to hold.

The cake ends arrive frozen, which is great as you can thaw only as much as you want to eat.

▼ The pack comes with stickers for jotting down the date you thaw it.

Each slice is about 16–17 centimetres (6.3–6.7 inches) long and a little over 1.5 centimetres (0.6 inches) thick, so it’s a generous serving.

After opening the pack and popping one of the slices on a plate, Natsuki cut it in half, which made it basically the same size as a regular piece of cake. Taking a taste, it was just as delicious as she’d hoped, with a dense yet fluffy sponge adding a soft sweetness to the fresh cream sandwiched inside of it.

The fresh cream was only mildly sweet, so Natsuki felt like she could easily eat to her heart’s content, and the flavours were incredibly well-balanced, which is a sign of a well-made, high-quality sweet.

▼ So this is what First Class tastes like!

While the cake can be eaten as is, because the flavour is simple, you can customise it to your liking. Natsuki chopped up the other half and added chocolate sauce, nuts and mint to make a decadent mini parfait, and it was utterly delicious.

With every mouthful, Natsuki felt like she was enjoying both a stylish cafe experience and a taste of first-class luxury in her own home. She now says she might just be hooked on these first-class cakes, and is chuffed that she found them.

If you’d like to enjoy a taste of first-class while not up in the air, these cakes can be purchased at the online store, as well as online retail sites like Amazon and Rakuten. According to the official website, a kilo of these cakes is equivalent to about 11 slices of shortcake, so at 3,999 yen (US$25.84), including postage, this is a very sweet deal.

title: Fox spotted in Tokyo’s 23 wards, Japanese Internet wonders if it’s a shapeshifting spirit [Video]
description: Foxes rarely venture this close to the Tokyo city center…unless kitsune spirits are here all the time. You can spot lots of representations of foxes in Tokyo. Fox spirit sculptures often guard the entrance to shrines, and with the Japanese word for fox, “kitsune,” also being a way to describe soba or udon noodles served […]
content:
Foxes rarely venture this close to the Tokyo city center…unless kitsune spirits are here all the time.

You can spot lots of representations of foxes in Tokyo. Fox spirit sculptures often guard the entrance to shrines, and with the Japanese word for fox, “kitsune,” also being a way to describe soba or udon noodles served with fried tofu as a topping, it’s not unusual to come across illustrated foxes on restaurant signs, menus, or instant noodle packaging.

▼ You might even spot a fox tail accessory on someone keeping classic gyaru fashion alive.

But a real-life fox, walking around on the streets of one of Tokyo’s 23 central wards? The deforestation of the downtown and downtown-adjacent area over the past few generations means that’s something you won’t see very often at all, but that’s exactly what appears in this video recorded in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward on the night of September 13.

Nerima is more or less the northwest of the congregation of Tokyo’s 23 wards, but while it’s not as developed as, say, Shinjuku, Shibuya, or Toshima Wards, it’s not a rural outpost either, especially in the neighborhood shown in the video. Much of Nerima consists of residential housing for people who commute deeper into downtown for school or work, and deforestation means it’s been many years since foxes were a common sight in the area.

▼ Nerima Ward

Now, the scientific explanation for the fox seen in the video is that it’s what zoologists call an “urban fox,” meaning a fox that’s adapted to finding food and shelter in ab area primarily habituated by humans. However, several online commenters have floated alternate theories drawing on Japanese folklore. According to legend, Japanese fox spirits have the ability to transform, and they sometimes take on the guise of humans and walk among us without anyone noticing, until they have a lapse in concentration and reveal their true form. With those stories in mind, comments on the video have included:

“Gotta be a young fox who’s still getting the hang of his transformation powers.”
“I bet he spends his afternoon as a hardworking salaryman.”
“Maybe he had a busy day and now he’s tired and forgot to keep up his transformation.”
“Probably changing back from his human form at the end of the day so that he can go do fox stuff.”
“I bet if you chased after him, you’d end up at a shrine.”
“Much happier to hear about this than another bear sighting.”
“’Urban Fox’ sounds cool! They should make a clothing brand called that.”
“Just like tanuki, there are kitsune who pretend to be humans living in the city.”
“It’s like something out of the Pompoko Ghibli anime.”

▼ For reference, the Ghibli movie Pompoko, about a group of shapeshifting tanuki losing their habitat due to the construction of a human housing development in the early 1990s, is set in the Tama New Town area, which is farther from the Tokyo city center than where the Nerima fox was seen.

▼ Tama New Town

The comments are most likely meant more as tongue-in-cheek jokes than actual belief in transforming spirits, but in all seriousness, as cute as foxes may be, it’s important to remember that foxes can be carriers of parasitic tapeworms which can be transmitted to humans and lead to the growth of harmful tumors on internal organs, and incubation periods of up to 15 years can complicate diagnosing a patient’s condition once they do start to show symptoms. In other words, contacting with a wild fox could be just as harmful as running afoul of the sinister fox spirits in the darker legends about them so if you do happen to come across a Tokyo kitsune, make sure to keep a respectful distance.

title: Gang of angry monkeys surrounds and attacks Japanese man in hot spring town
description: Morning walk interrupted by notorious Troop T1. The town of Yugawara, in Kanagawa Prefecture, seems like it should be a very tranquil place. A seaside hot spring town, with baths and inns dotting the cityscape as it stretches up into the mountains as you head inland, it’s the sort of setting that entices you to […]
content:
Morning walk interrupted by notorious Troop T1.

The town of Yugawara, in Kanagawa Prefecture, seems like it should be a very tranquil place. A seaside hot spring town, with baths and inns dotting the cityscape as it stretches up into the mountains as you head inland, it’s the sort of setting that entices you to get up early and go for a nice stroll, and that’s how last Thursday started off for one local resident in his 40s.

Unfortunately, at about 6:50 in the morning, as he was walking past the entrance to one of the town’s inns, the man was suddenly surrounded by a group of roughly a dozen antagonists. When you find yourself outnumbered to that degree, ordinarily the smart thing to do is to try to talk your way out of the situation. That wasn’t an option, though, because the man wasn’t surrounded by yakuza thugs or delinquent youths, but by angry monkeys.

The animals advanced on the man, biting him several times on his hands before he could either get away or scare them off, and after reporting the incident he was taken to the hospital for treatment for his injuries.

▼ Monkeys on the streets of Yugawara

The trouble that had found the man this day came in the form of violent members of the group known as Troop T1, and if you’re thinking that a group of monkeys needs to acquire a certain degree of infamy, or at least notoriety, before a town gives them a name, you’re right. Monkeys in Yugawara have been growing increasingly bold. As you can see in the above video, they’re not limiting themselves to forested areas, with many of the animals now feeling comfortable roaming around more developed parts of the town. In 2025, there were over 900 reported incidents of monkeys behaving in an aggressive or intimidating manner towards human residents of Yugawara, including a farmer who said he was accosted by a group of monkeys in his field while harvesting melons and citrus fruits.

▼ Video from last winter, demonstrating how little apprehension some of the monkeys feel around people. In addition to raiding gardens, the animals have broken into homes by tearing through screen doors or prying open sliding glass ones.

As a hot spring town, tourism is a vital part of Yugawara’s economy, and as a rural town, many of its residents are elderly. Troop T1 preying on unsuspecting tourists or defenseless senior citizens. Since at least last year, the city administration has been seeking authorization from the Kanagawa prefectural government to capture all of Troop T1, but permission to do so has yet to be finalized.

It’s not clear what’s causing the increased aggression from the animals. Decades ago, it wasn’t uncommon for tourists to bring food into the Yugawara foothills to feed the monkeys with, which could erode the animals’ fear of humans and see them, and their living spaces, as sources of sustenance, but this has become far less prevalent than it used to be. All the same, the local authorities have reminded everyone to neither feed nor provoke the monkeys, and to contact the police should they spot groups of the animals in town.

On the bright side, at least Yugawara hasn’t had any bear troubles.

title: Studio Ghibli releases new anime socks that pay tribute to characters from four different movies
description: Cosy up in colder weather with cute characters cuddling your toes. content:
Cosy up in colder weather with cute characters cuddling your toes.

With the days now getting colder in Japan, it’s time to start looking for cosy socks, and for Ghibli fans there’s no better way to stay warm than with some of the studio’s characters adorning your toes.

This year, Ghibli specialty shop chain Donguri Kyowakoku is giving fans a giant hug in the form of two new sock ranges, with the first being a collection of embroidered socks, honouring four of the studio’s popular movies.

These socks come with a cute little embroidered patch on the side, with cable-knit details giving each pair an elegant and stylish look.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro

The embroidering on the My Neighbour Totoro socks feature a circle of leaves to evoke the film’s forest setting, and in the middle is the Small Totoro, alongside a couple of acorns.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service

These socks feature Jiji, recalling the moment when the charismatic black cat steps in to act like a wide-eyed plush toy in a basket to help Kiki out when a mishap occurs during one of her deliveries.

▼ Spirited Away

This charming pair depicts Yu-bird, in tiny fly-like form, with a tea setting that recalls the visit to Zeniba’s house.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle

Sophie is the inspiration for this design, with the character being referenced through the long ponytail, distinctive hat, and milliner’s tools in honour of the millinery where she works.

The second range consists of a duo of “warm room socks“, which extend higher than the embroidered collection for a little more warmth and comfort.

▼ Spirited Away Warm Room Socks

This pair features Boh Mouse, with a scattering of star-like konpeito – the candies carried by the Soot Sprites – adding extra charm and colour to the design.

Both room socks come with a non-slip backing to prevent you from sliding about, even on hardwood floors.

▼ My Neighbour Totoro Warm Room Socks

Totoro is the star of the show on this design, with the creature’s beloved acorns making an appearance as well.

Both collections are made with a cotton-polyester blend and come in 23-25 centimetre (9-9.8-inch) sizes only. The embroidered socks retail for 880 yen (US$5.63) each, while the room socks retail for 1,320 yen each, and they can all be purchased at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) while stocks last.

title: Japanese convenience store is very focused with its new bento…maybe TOO focused
description: Lawson’s crazy corn bento arrives as part of new series of “sugi” foods. In Japanese, the suffix -sugi translates literally as “too” or “too much,” but it can also be used in the sense of “very.” This can sometimes make the intended meaning hard to understand. For example, if someone says their coworker isn’t just […]
content:
Lawson’s crazy corn bento arrives as part of new series of “sugi” foods.

In Japanese, the suffix -sugi translates literally as “too” or “too much,” but it can also be used in the sense of “very.” This can sometimes make the intended meaning hard to understand. For example, if someone says their coworker isn’t just yasahii (“kind”), but yasashisugi, that could either mean that they’re incredibly considerate, or it could mean that they’re overly, even problematically accommodating.

So generally you have to look at the overall context in which -sugi is being used, but even then, it’s not always easy to tell. For example, Japanese convenience store Lawson is getting set to release its new Ittentoppasugi line of bento boxed lunches. Ittentoppa basically means “single-minded,” which leaves us with the question of whether they’re extremely single-minded or too single-minded, and really, you could make an argument either way.

“JUST CORN” (コーンだけ), Lawson trumpets proudly in the promotional image for the new Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Yaki Tomorokoshi, which, despite its lengthy name, really is just a whole lot of roasted corn (yaki tomorokoshi) served over a tray of rice (shikitsume Gohan). Those are the only ingredients, aside from the buttery soy sauce spread over the kernels.

But maybe you look at that box of corn and rice and can’t help thinking you’d like something with a little more protein? No problem, because Lawson’s focused/obsessive offerings continue with the Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Teriyaki Sausage.

▼ As unartful as the presentation might be, teriyaki sauce and sausage actually are kind of a novel combination.

And finally, rounding out the Ittentoppasugi series is the Ittentoppasugi Shikitsume Gohan Bodakko, featuring a type of salted salmon popular in Akita Prefectue.

This one doesn’t match the quantity of its corn and sausage brethren, but it’s no less single-minded, perhaps to a depressingly spartan-looking degree. Speaking of which, Lawson describes all three of these as “bento,” which more commonly brings to mind boxed lunches with rice and a variety of side dishes (though bento does also sometimes get used for single-topping boxes/trays of rice too).

Now, if you’re someone who can’t get enough corn or sausage, or who appreciates salmon so much that you don’t want anything else getting in the way on your palate, then these Ittentoppasugi bento aren’t necessarily too ittentoppasugi, and for those who’re OK with this degree of single-mindedness, they are pretty reasonably priced. The corn and salmon bento are just 297 yen (US$1.85), and the sausage bento is 397 yen, far cheaper than just about any other convenience store bento these days.

On the other hand, some people are already voicing their opinion that Lawson has gone overboard with how laser-focused these concepts are, as shown in online comments such as:

“This is terrible. It’s like they just spread out a rice ball.”
“This is simple-sugi…and I’m intrigued.”
“You can just go ahead and write ‘Luxuries are forbidden’ on the packaging.”
“Thank you, Lawson, for taking pity on us poor people. I’ll be buying these.”
“That’s not single-minded, it’s shocking…I can’t get onboard with this.”
“Shouldn’t they leave this kind of stuff to the Lawson 100-yen [discount sister chain]?”

Lawson is actually also launching a line of luxurious zeitaku Zeitakusugi items at the same time, such as extra-meaty hiyashi chuka cold noodles with roast, stewed, and grilled pork (797 yen) and a whole box of Mont Blanc made with candied Japanese chestnuts (786 yen), though they don’t quite match the -sugi levels of the single-minded bento.

The Ittentoppasugi sausage and salmon both go on sale September 22, and the corn bento joins them one week later, on the 29th. Lawsone says they’ll all be on available “while supplies last,” though it doesn’t specify whether that’s referring to store stocks or the world supply of corn and sausage.

title: Japanese sweet potato ice cream season! Häagen-Dazs and Muji take different paths to our hearts
description: Two completely different ways to make a delicious Japanese autumn dessert. Now that we’re into the back half of September, we’re ready to switch our sweets snacking into autumn mode. And just like how farmers are harvesting their sweet potatoes, so too is it time for us to start bringing in Japan’s sweet potato ice […]
content:
Two completely different ways to make a delicious Japanese autumn dessert.

Now that we’re into the back half of September, we’re ready to switch our sweets snacking into autumn mode. And just like how farmers are harvesting their sweet potatoes, so too is it time for us to start bringing in Japan’s sweet potato ice creams for taste testing.

Today we’re looking at two ice cream makers with very different approaches. First, we’ve got Häagen-Dazs, a premium brand that’s very comfortable with adding decadent opulence to its desserts. But we’re also trying the new sweet potato ice cream from Mujirushi Ryohin, a.k.a. Muji, the lifestyle chain whose ice cream tends to be simple and understated, much like its furniture and housewares.

So, without further ado, let’s get started.

While Häagen-Dazs Japan brings out seasonal fall flavors on an annual basis, sweet potato isn’t always one of them. So we’d been getting a little anxious, but on September 15 they released their new Nou Mitsu Imo, or “Rich Sweet Potato,” flavor.

Pop the lid off, and you’re instantly greeted by a luxuriously lustrous glistening gold sweet potato sauce meant to evoke the sweet caramelized juices that ooze out of a freshly roasted sweet potato. The sauce is made with two of Japan’s most delicious sweet potato varieties, Beni Haruka (the sweetest variety in Japan) and anno imo.

Meanwhile, Mujirushi’s sweet potato ice cream flavor is just called Beni Haruka, and its English name, Sweet Potato Frozen Dessert, is starker still.

That name probably doesn’t have you expecting dazzling visuals, and sure enough, things are pretty plain under the lid.

▼ Hmm…those black dots do look intriguing, though…

In terms of visuals, there’s no denying that Häagen-Dazs is more attention-grabbing, and that’s where our spoon went first. True to its name, the Nou Mitsu Imo is rich and delicious. The sauce is thick but smooth, harmonizing excellently with the flavor and texture of the Beni Haruka ice cream, which has a bright yellow color to it.

With desserts that use this much sauce, you might be tempted to think they’re trying to cover up something or beat your taste buds into submission, but that’s not the case here. For all of its visual extravagance, Häagen-Dazs’ Nou Mitsu Imo is actually pretty straightforward. There are no ill-advised hidden ingredients or too-clever-for-its-own-good tricks involved, just lots and lots of great sweet potato flavor.

So after all that, would Mujirushi’s sweet potato ice cream come up short? Not at all! Remember those black dots we mentioned? It turns out they’re black sesame, and they’re not the only surprise that was waiting for us. As we dug down below the surface, we started coming across bits of actual sweet potato mixed in among the cream.

In addition to flavor, the sweet potato pieces added a lot of interesting texture, a crisp iciness with a fluffy chewiness waiting at the center. The black sesame imparted an elegantly enticing aroma, neither overpowering nor getting lost in the buttery notes of the sweet potato ice cream. All in all, it really delivers on the promise of “making the most of the ingredients’ flavors,” Mujirushi’s stated philosophy for its ice cream line.

Price-wise, there’s not much difference between the two, with Häagen-Dazs Nou Mitsu Imo at 373 yen (US$2.35) being just a touch more expensive than the 350-yen Mujirushi Beni Haruka. Muji’s ice cream is about 30 percent bigger (120 milliliters [4.1 ounce] vs. 90 milliliters), so it is technically the better value, but we think we can find room for both of these in our budget and stomach this fall.

title: Only two Yoshinoya branches in all of Japan are on a train platform, and this is one of them
description: Gyudon on the go in Kyobashi Station. Since they both use the same sort of broth, the logistics of keeping a pot of it heated and […]
content:
Gyudon on the go in Kyobashi Station.

When you spot a restaurant on a train platform in Japan, the odds are extremely high that it’s going to be a noodle joint, and specifically a soba/udon one. Since they both use the same sort of broth, the logistics of keeping a pot of it heated and always having batches of noodles boiling makes it pretty easy to serve up meals in a speedy fashion.

But while he was passing through Osaka’s Kyobashi Station the other day, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spotted something he couldn’t recall ever seeing anywhere else: a station platform Yoshinoya.

This appears to be one of only two station platform Yoshinoya’s in all of Japan. Curious to see if it pares down its selection to just the bare-bones basics for easier operations, Seiji stepped inside and took a look at the ordering touch screen, but nope, this branch looks to offer the same full menu as other Yoshinoyas that aren’t five steps away from where commuters and travelers are getting on or off trains.

▼ Whether you want just a standard beef bowl or the deluxe, limited-time combo meal with grilled unagi (eel), stewed gyudon beef, miso soup, and a salad, the Kyobashi Station Yoshinoya’s cooks are ready to accommodate you.

OK, so they’ve got the regular menu, and also the regular Yoshinoya prices, with no extra price gouging despite the convenience of being right on the platform. But does this unconventional setup mean that the quality suffers?

Not a bit! Seiji’s beef bowl was 100-percent as delicious as the ones he’s had at regular Yoshinoya branches.

Because of all that, eating at the Kyobashi Station Yoshinoya is a surreal mix of everyday and unusual vibes. The familiar food looks, tastes, and costs the same as it would at any other Yoshinoya. But look up from your beef bowl, and you’ll see trains coming and going in front of you without having to get up from your seat at the counter.

And while all Yoshinoya branches accept payment by tapping a Suica or other prepaid train fare card, it feels like an especially appropriate way to settle your bill here.

This Yoshinoya is located on Kyobashi Station’s Osaka Loop Line outer track platform, and it’s open morning, noon, and night every day, not just during weekday rush hours. As for the only other train platform Yoshinoya in Japan, it’s on Platform 4 of Meitetsu Nagoya Station in Nagoya, a town with at least one more noteworthy platform dining option too.

title: Three Daiso ideas for a super-cheap but still cool (or cute) Halloween look
description: Further proof that no matter what we need, we can probably find it at Japan’s favorite 100 yen store. Japan has embraced the frights, fun, and food of Halloween in a big way in recent years, but still not in a complete mirror of how things are done in America. For example, Japan doesn’t anything […]
content:
Further proof that no matter what we need, we can probably find it at Japan’s favorite 100 yen store.

Japan has embraced the frights, fun, and food of Halloween in a big way in recent years, but still not in a complete mirror of how things are done in America. For example, Japan doesn’t anything equivalent to Spirit Halloween or other temporary discount specialty shops that move into vacant shopping mall spaces to offer costumes ideas ahead of October 31.

So what should you do if you find yourself in need of a quick, affordable Halloween outfit that’s still some mix of creepy, cute, or cool? Head to Daiso, Japan’s favorite 100 yen store chain.

That’s what our Japanese-language reporter Natuski Goto did, since as of September Daiso is stocked with Halloween items. Because wallet-friendly shopping is Daiso’s whole deal, Natsuki decided to keep her Halloween outfit decidedly low-cost, limiting herself to three budget points: 110, 220, and 550 yen (roughly US$0.70, US$1.40, and US$3.50), even accounting for Japan’s 10-percent sales tax.

Let’s see what she put together.

● 110-yen budget

When you’re limiting yourself to just a single item, you’ve got to pick something that provides a big impact, and Natsuki’s pick is Daiso’s Skull Mask.

Officially, this is the “Skull Mask -Color-,” as it’s got a faux metallic sheen to it with a distressed effect that makes it look like it was dragged through a dungeon, graveyard, or some other suitably spooky scenery. With a simple single head strap, this mask only covers the front of your face, so it works best paired with a hoody to help sell the skull illusion, and a black garment gives you a nice shinigami/death god vibe.

One thing to be aware of, though, is that as a one-size-fits-all mask, the eyeholes may be a little on the large size for some wearers. Because of that, your eyes might need to do some acting to suitably match the dark depravity of that ghoulish grin, but at a price that’s less than a bottle of tea from a vending machine (and much less than a can of vending machine hot pot), this mask is pretty impressive.

● 220-yen budget

Shifting gears to the cute category, Natsuki’s pick for the mid-range of extremely low budgets is a bit of cat cosplay. Daiso actually has a variety of Halloween-themed hairbands, some featuring quirky pumpkins or naughty devil horns, but with enough money in this budget tier for a second item, Natsuki says the “Cat Headband” is the best choice because of the potential to pair it with Daiso’s crayon-style face paint set.

The Face Crayons are incredibly easy to use, with a tactile feel pretty much the same as coloring on paper, just that you’re using them on your skin. You get four colors in the set, and since they’ll work just as well on your arms, you could also use them to make a zombie costume by giving yourself an array of scars or bloody wounds.

But like we said, Natsuki’s preferred way to use them is to give herself the whiskers and nose of a friendly kitty.

Of course, you could skip the face-painting and wear just the hairband, which would put this costume into the 110-yen budget space. With cat ears being a common motif among the otaku/YouTuber crowd, though, taking the little extra time to add some whiskers does a lot to make this look feel like something special for Halloween.

● 550-yen budget

Part of Halloween’s expanding popularity is that a lot of times you might want yourself looking to get in on the fun but without the impracticality of wearing full-on costume elements. So for those times, Natsuki’s 550-yen Daiso Halloween look is something that you can easily do for fun photos with friends or family regardless of your wardrobe. Daiso has all sorts of Halloween hair clips, so Natsuki grabbed four of those, plus a pack of body stickers.

▼ The bow with a zombie hand coming out of it is especially clever.

After a few minutes of arranging them, Natsuki was giving off a selfie-worthy Halloween aura.

With more than a month to go until Halloween, there’s still plenty of time for hardcore costumers to sort out more involved and extravagant costumes. But for those who simply want to get into the spirit of the season in a lighthearted way, or who get invited to a last-minute Halloween party and need to put something together on their way from the office, Daiso is definitely worth checking out.

title: Tokyo cafe challenges customers to play with their food? Challenge accepted!
description: Riding the waves and eating the sweets in Asagaya. It’s been said that you can learn everything you really need to know in life in kindergarten, but that’s obviously oversimplifying things quite a bit. Adult life presents problems far more complex than the topics handled in a curriculum designed for five-year-olds. For example, from a […]
content:
Riding the waves and eating the sweets in Asagaya.

It’s been said that you can learn everything you really need to know in life in kindergarten, but that’s obviously oversimplifying things quite a bit. Adult life presents problems far more complex than the topics handled in a curriculum designed for five-year-olds. For example, from a young age pretty much everyone gets taught not to play with their food…but what do you do when the people who’re giving you that food not only encourage you to play with it, but outright challenge you to?

That’s the philosophical question represented by dessert cafe Tokyo Taiyaki Mania. There’s a lot of accuracy in that name, as the shop is indeed located in Tokyo (in the Asagaya neighborhood, to be precise), and the staff is passionate about taiyaki, the traditional Japanese desserts of fish-shaped cakes filled with anko (sweet bean paste) or other sweet stuff.

And yet, Tokyo Taiyaki Mania’s name isn’t completely thorough. It leaves out roughly half of the menu options: the gelato that Tayaki Mania (as we’ll call the place for short) produces in-house, using an ice cream-making machine imported from Italy.

This brings us to another temptation to go against something we were taught as kids: Don’t spoil your appetite by eating too many sweets. As adults, though, we’ve learned that eating double desserts isn’t “spoiling your appetite” so much as “using your appetite’s full potential in the most joy-inducing way possible,” and thankfully Taiyaki Mania agrees and recommends treating yourself to both a taiyaki and some ice cream at the same time.

In turn, this, leads to the natural compulsion to combine the treats, and once again, Taiyaki Mania isn’t about to try to talk you out of that. As a matter of fact, the cafe’s website invites customers to take the “naminori (wave-riding) challenge” by balancing their taiyaki atop their swirl of gelato and snapping a photo of the surfing-style sweets.

This was a challenge our taste-testing Japanese-language reporter Yayoi Saginomiya was happy to accept, especially since she’d opted for the photogenic and appropriately colored Blue Ocean flavor of ice cream.

That said, balancing the taiyaki is easier said than done. The gelato isn’t watery, but it’s still a creamy dessert, so it’ll start to melt if you wait too long. For best results Yayoi recommends standing the taiyaki more or less upright at the top of the swirl, evenly distributing its weight over the densest concentration of ice cream.

▼ Success!

OK, so the wave-riding taiyaki combo looks great, but how does it taste? Yayoi says she was very impressed. In terms of ingredients. Taiyaki Mania does things differently than conventional sweets shops, using no wheat flour in their batter. Instead, the cake is made from a mixture of rice flour and tofu, and the anko inside contains beet sugar instead of refined white sugar. Similarly, their gelato is gluten-free and entirely non-dairy.

Whether Taiyaki Mania’s ingredient philosophy is attractively health-conscious or a form of sweets sacrilege is a matter of personal perspective, but Yayoi found the results quite tasty, producing a light and straightforward sweetness with a clean finish. The flavor of the Blue Hawaii ice cream, like many blue desserts in Japan, is what’s called “soda” in Japanese, referring not to cola but to a light apple citrus cider, and it also has a pinch of salt to give it an extra maritime-evocative element.

Taiyaki Mania’s prices are on the premium side, with our mini taiyaki costing us 378 yen (US$2.40) and our gelato 918 yen. As an added bonus, though, Taiyaki Mania is also a little more stylish than the typical taiyaki stand, and it’s located along a covered shopping street that’s fun to stroll along and get a peek at daily Tokyoite life.

And don’t worry, neither they, nor we, will tattle to your mom about you playing with your food.

title: Car-floating sheets selling well to cope with increasing flood risk in Japan
description: If you can’t beat them, float on them. As in many corners of the globe, Japan has been putting up with an increasing number of previously rare weather-related natural disasters. One of the more surprising was the widespread flooding around Chiba after torrential rains fell from a line of squall clouds that inexplicably stopped moving […]
content:
If you can’t beat them, float on them.

As in many corners of the globe, Japan has been putting up with an increasing number of previously rare weather-related natural disasters. One of the more surprising was the widespread flooding around Chiba after torrential rains fell from a line of squall clouds that inexplicably stopped moving for a while.

▼ Many people were caught while out driving and had to abandon their cars on the street after the water caused them to stall.

In addition to 13 deaths, the amount of damage it caused was massive. Some estimates say over 10,000 vehicles were damaged, many beyond repair, from being completely submerged in filthy water.

With such valuable property at risk of becoming useless at any moment from increasingly unpredictable weather, many people are searching for ways to protect their cars from flooding. One such way appeared in the form of SAM-CS (“Sam Car Sheet”).

SAM-CS works by covering your car in plastic sheets that allow the car to float when flooding occurs. It takes about 10 minutes to set up and involves parking your car on the bottom sheet, which fastens to the sides with suction cups. Then, another sheet goes over top to block rain from entering.

There’s also an optional, but highly recommended, set of straps that prevent the car from floating away or into something else that would cause damage. The product costs 88,000 yen ($560) for a mid-sized car, which seems like a lot for some plastic sheets but is a sound investment compared to the cost of repairing or losing a car.

SAM-CS was originally developed back in 2024, at which time its maker, Onoda Sangyo, was only getting about two inquiries a month. But after the Chiba flooding, they’ve gotten 30 calls in the past two weeks.

When news of the product’s recent demand hit the Internet, there was a surprising number of negative comments. That being said, many critics didn’t seem to have read the explanation fully, while others tended to lack sufficient understanding of how cars, flammable gases, or the law work.

“Won’t it just float away?”
“Looks like a pain to set up.”
“By the time you realize you need it, it’d probably be too late.”
“What happens if it drifts away and damages someone’s house?”
“They should make machines that you drive through to wrap your car like this, like they have with car wash machines.”
“I would just pump air into the car until there’s so much pressure the water can’t get in.”
“We should just fill the tires with hydrogen and make cars float that way.”
“Once the car stops touching the ground, ownership rights transfer to whoever takes it. You could just go around collecting cars.”
“I’d rather spend the money on a Switch 2.”

Most people probably would rather spend the money on a Switch 2 than a car condom, but there often come times in our lives where we have to decide between what we want and what we need. And since GTAVI is still unconfirmed for the Switch 2, it’d probably be more prudent to opt for the protection against debilitating vehicle damage.

title: The number of centenarians living in Japan tops 100,000 for the first time
description: Perhaps even more impressively, it’s also the 56th consecutive year that centenarian numbers have broken records. 100 is an impressive number on its own, especially when you see it laid out in some kind of visual form. 100 coins, 100 books, 100 days on a calendar…you’re probably running out of physical room to display whatever […]
content:
Perhaps even more impressively, it’s also the 56th consecutive year that centenarian numbers have broken records.

100 is an impressive number on its own, especially when you see it laid out in some kind of visual form. 100 coins, 100 books, 100 days on a calendar…you’re probably running out of physical room to display whatever it is. However, let’s now multiply that number by 1,000 to arrive at 100,000–a virtually incomprehensible number from a visual standpoint, but one that’s now connected to a new population record in Japan.

Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare recently announced that as of September 1, there’s a record number of 107,677 centenarians living in Japan–which is up 7,914 people from the previous year and is the first time the number has surpassed 100,000. For reference, when the Ministry began tracking numbers in 1963, there were only 153 documented centenarians, and the number surpassed 50,000 for the first time in 2012. Currently, the oldest living woman is 114-year-old Fuyo Kishimoto of Kyoto City and the oldest living man is 112-year-old Hikaru Kato of Kumamoto City.

▼ We’re gonna need a bigger cake for all of those candles.

Out of this year’s record number, 94,298 of them are women–which is just shy of 90 percent–while 13,379 are men. It also includes a combined 54,294 foreign nationals and permanent residents of Japan, with 45,769 women and 8,525 men. That’s also the highest number ever recorded, with a 1,984-person increase since last year as the proportion of foreign populations within Japan continue to grow.

Nationally, for every 10,000 people in Japan, the average number of centenarians is 87.51. Prefectures with the highest average of them are Shimane with 186.65, Kochi with 169.52, and Tottori with 152.48. Prefectures with the fewest average of them are Saitama with 51.27, Aichi with 57.79, and Osaka with 60.06.

▼One present for every birthday would take up a lot of table space.

This new data is timely for Respect for the Aged Day, a public holiday in Japan celebrated this year on September 21. With many cities rethinking how to celebrate the birthdays of their older residents given the increasing numbers of them, we can only hope that Japan’s birthday candle business can also keep up with them all.

title: Emperor of Japan poses for photo with Studio Ghibli’s No Face [Video]
description: Japan’s reigning monarch and his sweetheart get into the spirit of Ghibli Park. Theme parks are popular date spots in Japan, and Ghibli Park is no exception. On any given day you can expect to see lots of couples strolling around the Aichi Prefecture park and soaking up the atmosphere, and with Ghibli anime being […]
content:
Japan’s reigning monarch and his sweetheart get into the spirit of Ghibli Park.

Theme parks are popular date spots in Japan, and Ghibli Park is no exception. On any given day you can expect to see lots of couples strolling around the Aichi Prefecture park and soaking up the atmosphere, and with Ghibli anime being loved and respected by people of all ages in Japan, it’s not just teen sweethearts who want to snap photos with characters and scenery from the studio’s films.

So, ordinarily, there wouldn’t have been anything unusual about a 66-year-old man and his 62-year-old wife asking someone to take a picture of them with Spirited Away’s No Face using the husband’s smartphone. Even the couple’s name, Naruhito and Masako, aren’t particularly noteworthy, being fairly common for people of their ages.

And yet, this was a very special occasion, because the Naruhito and Masako in question are the emperor and empress of Japan.

Japan’s reigning monarchs stopped by Ghibli Park on the second morning of their two-day visit to Aichi Prefecture. The park’s unique layout consists of a number of separated zones all located within the larger Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, and the above video shows the couple touring the Ghibli’s Grand Warehouse section. In addition to a collection of Ghibli artwork and production displays, this part of the park houses Becoming Characters in Memorable Ghibli Scenes, a series of diorama-like recreations of memorable moments from Ghibli anime, including the train ride from Spirited Away, where Emperor Naruhito asked an aide to take a photo of him and his wife with No Face using the royal smartphone.

The video also shows the couple being guided through the area by a man wearing a black polo shirt. This was no random Ghibli Park employee, but instead Goro Miyazaki, son of Ghibli co-founder Hayao Miyazaki and the person most responsible for Ghibli Park’s design and operational philosophy.

After saying hi to No Face, the emperor and empress met with local elementary school children in Ghibli Grand Warehouse’s Catbus play room. As you can see in the video, though, the park’s rule of the Catbus itself being off-limits to adults apparently applies even to the emperor, as Naruhito and Masako both stayed in the adults-allowed part of the room while talking with the kids.

With the royal couple also attending an Asian Games 2026 women’s basketball game between Japan and Kazakhstan at Aichi Arena later that day, it’s unclear how much of the rest of Ghibli Park they were able to see. It’s also not known if they were able to attend a screening of the newest Ghibli anime, which can’t be seen anywhere else in the world other than the park, but if you want to see it, it’ll be having an extra-special outdoor showing in October.

title: My night trapped in Nagoya’s flood: what do you do when Japan’s trains shut down?
description: Here is essential advice for surviving sudden disaster in Japan. On September 8, 2026, the regions of Chubu, the center of Japan, were struck by an aggressive autumn front that unleashed a sudden and immense downpour, resulting in one of the highest levels of rain the area has seen since records began. The streets of […]
content:
Here is essential advice for surviving sudden disaster in Japan.

On September 8, 2026, the regions of Chubu, the center of Japan, were struck by an aggressive autumn front that unleashed a sudden and immense downpour, resulting in one of the highest levels of rain the area has seen since records began. The streets of Nagoya and railways became rivers, and the subway stations became pools, halting any and all public transport, leaving commuters and travelers stranded with no way to return home. Thankfully, there were only minimal injuries and no fatalities.

Now, for those that may not have already guessed from my love of red miso, this is where I live and work, so I was personally affected by this upheaval. When I am not sequestering myself with my computer to write articles about dancing on noodles and crabs being used for burglaries, I engage in more traditional work and commuting. At 4:13 p.m., my phone started beeping at me, which in Japan is usually a sign of impending earthquakes, so preparing myself to take protective measures, I glanced at the alert to find that it was for a landslide (dosha saigai, 土砂詐害). “A peculiar alert for an urban city,” I thought, as I moved to the window, only to be surprised at how heavy the rain was.

▼ My phone’s alert history from September 8

Soon, alerts bombarded my phone, updating me on the situation, and I soon saw something that I had never seen before: the highest “Level Five” warning (tokubetsu keiho, 特別警報). Level Five indicates that somewhere within the region a disaster is imminent or has already occurred, so evacuation is too late and people should take immediate life-saving action on site, such as evacuating to a higher floor. In the case of the Nagoya flooding, it was the Shonai River and Yada River that run through the city that were at risk of breaching their banks (hanran, 氾濫), as well as other smaller rivers.

▼ Shonai River

I checked the public transport, through the train line’s website, only to find that no trains were running for the rest of the day, meaning I could not get home. On the bright side, my workplace is fairly high up in the building, so I was pretty safe from my vantage point, where I could no longer see the streets I normally walked for the rivers flowing through them (submerged, kansui, 冠水).

However, that left me with a little conundrum of how to spend the night. There was still the option of getting a hotel near my company, but the prices had shot up and the company would not cover it (cheapskates). So, I could either go to an emergency shelter or hunker down at my workplace. Considering the possible crowdedness of the shelters, I opted for my workplace, so I procured some materials to make a temporary bed, spent the night, and was ready for work bright and early the next morning. Fortunately, by the time it was ready to clock off, the train lines had reopened, so I could finally get back home for a shower and decent sleep.

Considering my situation, I felt I was pretty lucky with how everything turned out, but it got me thinking about all the people who might have been traveling through Nagoya and suddenly found themselves without a home, hotel, or way to get to their destination, and how they fared.

If you find yourself in a situation like mine, the experience can be deeply disorienting for people not used to Japan’s sudden disasters, and even though the country routinely deals with natural crises, events such as this can instantly disrupt the status quo. It is necessary to understand local warning protocols and how to react when public transportation grounds to a halt, leaving you stranded and unable to go anywhere (kitaku konnan, 帰宅困難). Even if there are no impending typhoons or inclement weather, it is still useful to be aware of this information for any eventuality.

Remember that Level Five notification I received? Well, Japan’s Meteorological Agency uses a five-level disaster alert system that serves as the baseline for all official guidance. One and Two are just your routine news and weather checks, but once Level Three hits, seniors and vulnerable individuals are advised to evacuate, and Level Four commands an immediate evacuation for everyone in designated hazard zones. If your route to the official shelter is impeded due to rising floodwaters (kozui, 洪水), like how it was around my building, it is actually recommended to evacuate vertically, going to the second floor or higher of a concrete building rather than venturing outside.

▼ No matter how good you are at swimming, stay inside.

Earthquake evacuations are slightly different, in that you should try to avoid going to a building until it is confirmed safe. In the event you are already inside of a building, take cover under a sturdy desk, and only move outside if there is an active threat of building collapse, gas leaks or fire. If you are outside, instead make your way carefully to a large, open space, like a park or school grounds.

I was pretty fortunate to be stuck at my workplace, but had I been out exploring an unfamiliar neighborhood, the strategy I took would have been pretty different. If you find yourself caught out in the open during a storm, head toward a major train station, municipal building, or large shopping mall. These structures serve as community hubs and designated shelters during emergencies. If you are not sure where to go, asking “Hinanjo wa doko desu ka?” (“Where is the shelter?”) will direct you to the nearest shelter, and stating “Tasukete kudasai” (“Please help me”) in an urgent situation will clearly communicate that you require immediate assistance. Other helpful phrases can be printed off and made into cards from the Japan National Tourism Organization’s (JNTO) Safety Tips website here.

▼ “Don’t panic. The shelter is over here.”

My initial instinct when I saw the train suspensions (unten miawase, 運転見合わせ), was to figure out a way home anyway. Perhaps I could walk or rent a bicycle? But stepping out into flooded streets carries risks, be it from hidden manholes or blocking emergency vehicles. If you’re stuck at a station, look out for announcements of refuge shelters (taihi shisetsu, 退避施設) or temporary waiting facilities (ichiji taiki basho, 一時待機場所), which are safe indoor spaces in stations and commercial centers where staff distribute supplies and updates.

▼ Supplies can include: water, a blanket, a biscuit, and a portable toilet.

These temporary waiting facilities usually get announced once they are opened, so looking at a live map (like this one for Nagoya) is a great way to check the location and level of crowdedness of each facility, just search for information from the city or ward you are in. However, if you’re stranded in Tokyo, a service called Kitakon DX has recently started, allowing people to easily register for temporary accommodation and provide directions to that location.

Had I not been at work with its free but annoyingly intermittent Wi-Fi connection, I might have not had the ability to contact my family to let them know I was safe. However, Japan is no stranger to natural disasters, so the country activates a free emergency Wi-Fi network under the universal SSID “00000JAPAN”. Connecting to this network does not require a password, allowing stranded travelers to access emergency apps and let your loved ones know that you are safe. There is also the 24/7 multi-lingual tourist hotline operated by the JNTO (050-3816-2787), which is specifically designed for international travelers in accidents or emergencies, or you can contact the police emergency number 110, or the fire rescue and ambulance service on 119, both of which should have English-speaking staff available, just start the conversation with “English, please.”

If I met with a heavy storm in a foreign country, it would be a lie to say that I wouldn’t be panicking, so preparation is essential. Every resident and traveler should install key apps, such as the JNTO’s Safety Tips app, NERV Disaster Prevention, and NHK World-Japan, for multi-lingual real-time alerts. Additionally, carrying a lightweight emergency kit, containing a portable power bank, paper copies of your passport and other travel documents inside a sealed plastic bag, and physical cash in 1,000 yen bills and coins, ensures you remain less panicked even during a complete infrastructure shutdown and power outage.

Having extreme weather, or other natural disasters, pouncing on you unawares can feel daunting. They are an unpredictable reality of living in or visiting in Japan, but the country’s disaster response framework is well-oiled and designed to keep everyone safe, even if you do not speak the language. With a bit of awareness, a few apps, and a basic understanding of protocols, you can navigate even the stormiest of nights safely and calmly.

title: Studio Ghibli unveils new anime stationery collection, with a Spirited Away River God memo stand
description: The mysterious god even has a moving mouth, to eat the tasty anime meals on the note pads. As ardent lovers of both Studio Ghibli and Japanese stationery, we’re always very excited when the anime studio releases a stationery collection. So when Ghibli specialty chain Donguri Kyowakoku unveiled a brand new range of memo pads […]
content:
The mysterious god even has a moving mouth, to eat the tasty anime meals on the note pads.

As ardent lovers of both Studio Ghibli and Japanese stationery, we’re always very excited when the anime studio releases a stationery collection. So when Ghibli specialty chain Donguri Kyowakoku unveiled a brand new range of memo pads adorned in food from some of our favourite Ghibli anime, plus a stand designed to look like the River God from Spirited Away, we had to stop ourselves from immediately purchasing the whole collection and share the find with you straight away.

Starting with the memo pads, there are three to choose from, priced at 770 yen (US$4.93) each, and they all look delicious.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service Round Memo – Kiki’s Cake

As fans will know, the cake on this memo pad is the one that Kiki receives as a gift from Madame, and it’s been beautifully recreated.

Inside the cake, you’ll find a 100-sheet memo pad, with Kiki and Madame bringing a dash of joy and warmth to each page.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle Round Memo – Calcifer’s Bacon and Eggs

This memo pad features the sizzling bacon and eggs from Howl’s Moving Castle, which is beautifully printed so you can even see the smoke rising from the pan.

Inside, you’ll find 100 pages of Markl, happily gobbling up the meal, just as we would if it were placed before us.

▼ Ponyo on the Cliff by the Sea Round Memo – Lisa’s Ramen

Sosuke’s mum Lisa makes this iconic meal for him and Ponyo, bringing them comfort during a heavy storm.

The instant noodles, topped with thick slices of ham, a boiled egg, and green onions is one of the most delicious-looking meals in the Ghibli cannon, and with this pad on the table, we’ll be reminded of its deliciousness every day.

All the memo pads above have a a distinctive round shape, which Donguri Kyowakoku says has been “born from the bookbinding techniques of skilled craftsmen”. Manufactured by Movic, which operates under the umbrella of the Animate Group, which handles the planning, manufacturing and distribution of merchandise covering the world of anime, manga and video games, each pad is carefully designed for quality and ease of use.

▼ The most exciting product in the lineup for us, though, is the Spirited Away River God Memo Stand (4,950 yen).

Also produced by Movic, this stand is like a figurine, capturing the quiet, mysterious presence of the River God who appears out of the water during a pivotal moment in the bathhouse in Spirited Away.

Here, the River God acts as a memo stand, holding memos in the clip behind its head.

Although you can clip any type of paper into the stand, we’re tempted to tear a note out of the round memo pads and write the character’s iconic words, “Well done” on it for dramatic effect.

Adding to the drama is the character’s jaw, which actually moves, so you really can feel like it’s saying “Well done” whenever you finish a difficult task.

The interactive element is a very nice touch, and as it’s made of metal and quite weighty, it’s designed to put up with all your character roleplays.

▼ The stand is as solid as the presence of the character.

So if you’ll excuse us now, we’re off to make our purchase, and if you’d like to do the same, you can click on the links below to grab your favourites before they sell out!

title: Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword gets real-world practicality as a giant towel [Photos]
description: The fantasy of using Cloud’s sword every day can now become a reality. There’s a whole lot of imagery in anime and video games that looks awesome but would be impractical in the real world. Even within that artistic subgenre, though, Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword is an especially extreme example. Right off the bat, […]
content:
The fantasy of using Cloud’s sword every day can now become a reality.

There’s a whole lot of imagery in anime and video games that looks awesome but would be impractical in the real world. Even within that artistic subgenre, though, Final Fantasy VII’s Buster Sword is an especially extreme example.

Right off the bat, it’s a sword, something that most of us don’t have a use for in our daily lives. Should you somehow happen to have a melee weapon-intensive lifestyle, even then the Buster Sword isn’t a particularly viable choice, since while protagonist Cloud can swing the thing around with ease, it’d be too heavy and bulky to fight with for those of us who have to deal with actual weight and gravity without any assistance from an in-game physics engine.

And yet…the Buster Sword does look really cool, so thankfully Square Enix has come up with a version that can serve a useful purpose for those of us not living in the world of Final Fantasy.

Draped over that dude’s back is the Final Fantasy VII Buster Sword Muffler Towel. Muffler towels (muffler here being used to indicate a scarf, not a part of a car’s exhaust system) are essentially a long face towel, made of material that’s pliable enough to drape over your shoulders or wrap around your neck. A lot of muffler towels bear the names and insignias of sports teams, bands, or idol singers, but this one instead features a print of Cloud’s Buster Sword.

▼ The reverse-side has longer loops to better wick away moisture.

Muffler towels are especially popular at fan events, where dampening them with water before putting one on your shoulders is a great way to counteract the heat generated by large crowds. With a length of 128.5 centimeters (50.6 inches), though, the Buster Sword towel is large enough to make a striking statement as home décor, hung on a wall or next to a sink.

It’s available for preorder through the Square Enix online store here, priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50) and with a release date of December 19. Just make sure your cat doesn’t get it mixed up with its Buster Sword scratching pad.

title: Denny’s Mapputatsu? Parfait is hiding a big secret in plain sight that splits us down the middle
description: The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone. Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to […]
content:
The Mapputatsu? Parfait tackles food waste without sacrificing visuals so that you can still happily feed both yourself and your phone.

Back in January, a new style of parfait appeared at Denny’s Japan. From the front it appears as a regular parfait, but from the side, it looks like it’s been split in two–leading to its name, the Mapputatsu? Parfait (“Two equal parts? Parfait”).

▼ Pictured below are versions with Shine Muscat grapes for 1,078 yen (US$6.87) and with chocolate for 748 yen.

The purpose of this unusual setup is to reduce food waste while still providing a visually attractive, photo-worthy treat for diners. The menu even provides statistics that 54 percent of diners have ordered food for the sake of posting photos on social media and one out of three have left their dessert unfinished at family-style restaurants in Japan. With parfaits typically looking like veritable works of food art but also being on the larger side, we can assume that they’re one of the more common menu items that diners order for the visual spectacle but aren’t able to finish.

Initially, the Mapputatsu? Parfait was only available at two Denny’s Japan locations, but it’s been slowly expanding onto menus across the country. We happened to be in the area of Saitama-Shintoshin’s Cocoon City shopping complex branch recently and decided to swing by to finally try it out.

Once we sat down and peeked at the digital tablet menu, we were excited to see it in all of its question-asking glory. It was a tough choice but we ordered the Shine Muscat version.

It arrived about 10 minutes later. We took a moment to admire its striking visuals from head-on, the way the waiter had placed it down on the table in front of us.

Unsuspecting diners would never know…

…that the reverse side held a big secret: the parfait glass indeed looked like it had been split straight down the middle!

▼ Even the grapes were cleanly sliced in half.

Thankfully, that didn’t mean the glass was in any danger of collapsing, but just that the vessel was only half the width of a regular one.

We had a train to catch soon, so it was time to dig in. It was still blowing our minds that even viewed from the top it looked like a perfectly ordinary parfait.

The Shine Muscat grapes were, as usual, tantalizingly sweet and refreshing. They meshed wonderfully with the layers of sorbet and jelly lining the inside of the glass. It felt good to know that we were still getting everything that we would from a normal parfait.

The sweet treat as a whole was truly the perfect size to feel full in a comfortable–not sickly–way.

Some readers might be asking, “Why not just order a mini parfait instead?” Mini parfaits in smaller glass dishes also exist at Denny’s Japan, so that’s always a possibility. However, we have to admit that there’s something special about the thrill of having a tall parfait placed in front of you that a shorter one just can’t replace.

Please note that not all Denny’s Japan locations may offer the Mapputatsu? Parfait. Those that do may not have all the same versions, either, so it’s best to check ahead of time if there’s a specific flavor that you want. We would strongly recommend the Shine Muscat variety–in fact, it was so good that we’re now hooked on anything with the same taste!

title: Three amazing Japanese convenience store sweet potato desserts to eat right now (and 11 for later)
description: A roadmap for starting your journey of eating your way through Family Mart’s sweet potato sweets lineup. Though they usually have a little fruit and vegetable corner where you can pick up some bananas, a carrot, or half a head of lettuce, Japanese convenience stores aren’t really the best place to go if you’re looking […]
content:
A roadmap for starting your journey of eating your way through Family Mart’s sweet potato sweets lineup.

Though they usually have a little fruit and vegetable corner where you can pick up some bananas, a carrot, or half a head of lettuce, Japanese convenience stores aren’t really the best place to go if you’re looking for fresh seasonal produce. Japanese convenience stores are, on the other hand, exactly where you want to be if you’re looking for new seasonal sweets.

Sweet potato sweets season is here, and September 22 is essentially harvest day as Family Mart releases no fewer than 14 desserts that feature the flavor, and sometimes even the look, of sweet spuds. We realize that even the biggest sweets fans might have trouble fitting that many items into their snacking schedule, so our taste-testing reporter Natsuki Goto has sampled them all and prepared her personal list of the three she recommends eating first, then working your way to the rest if you have the time/stomach capacity.

3. Mocchi Oimo Bread (Beni Haruka) (185 yen [US$1.15])

This pillowy soft pastry visually mimics a roasted sweet potato that’s been sliced open, with an eye-catching contrast of colors to go with its hybrid design. While the outside has the texture of a soft bread bun, the inner section is a moist sponge cake, thanks to the use of sweet bean paste flavored with Beni Haruka, one of Japan’s sweetest varieties of sweet potato.

The sprinkling of black sesame seeds, a common addition to roasted sweet potatoes in Japan, adds a touch of mature sophistication, and the overall flavor is excellent. Family Mart brings out some sort of sweet potato bread pretty much every autumn, but this is one of their best yet, and anyone who likes sweet potatoes will find a lot to love here.

Before we move on to Natsuki’s number-two pick, let’s take a look at some of the also-rans in the lineup. Honestly, there wasn’t a bad-tasting treat in the bunch, so you can think of these as “not as amazing as the top three” rather than not being recommended.

▼ Caramel-scent Sweet Potato Croissant (185 yen)

▼ Satsuma Imo Sweet Potato Stick (180 yen per bag)

▼ Sweet Potato Dorayaki (216 yen)

▼ Sweet Potato Zakuhoro Cream Puff (254 yen)

▼ Sweet Potato Canelé with Caramel Sauce (285 yen)

▼ Beni Haruka Sweet Potato Terrine (298 yen)

OK, let’s get back to Natsuki’s top picks with…

2. Sweet Potato Florentine (195 yen)

Japan has a pretty broad palate in terms of desserts with overseas origins, but you don’t often see Florentines at convenience stores. For those unfamiliar with the term, Florentines are a kind of French biscuit-type cookie, coated with caramel and topped with nuts.

For this version, though, Family Mart swaps out the crushed nuts and replaces them with imo kenpi, crisp, candied sweet potato chips.

The result is an understatedly classy confectionary, which still retains a bit of a nutty nuance thanks to the aromatic caramel, plus the crunch of a conventional Florentine while adding a strong sweet potato sensation. The only complaint Natsuki has is that the Sweet Potato Florentine is a little on the small side, but it’s photogenic and very tasty, so it still gets an enthusiastic thumbs-up from her.

And before we reach the king of this hill of sweet potato desserts, let’s look at some of the other items in the lineup.

▼ Sweet Potato and Cheese Pizza Wrap (330 yen)

▼ Imo Kenpi Chocolate (286 yen)

▼ Caramel Sweet Potato Chips (248 yen)

▼ Drinkable Dairy Roasted Sweet Potato shake (278 yen)

▼ Beni Haruka Sweet Potato Monaka (225 yen)

And now, we finally come to Natsuki’s absolute, can’t-miss, number-one Family Mart sweet potato sweets pick, which is…

1. Sweet Potato Pound Cake (198 yen)

Once again the Beni Haruka sweet potato shows up to elevate this simple dessert to an exalted level, with Beni Haruka paste kneaded into the dough before baking, and chopped pieces of sweet potato added in too.

Aside from the bright, inside-of-a-sweet-potato color, there’s nothing fancy about the visuals, but that’s fine because this cake is all about pleasing the taste buds, and it does that magnificently. Family Mart actually offered a similar item last year, but the 2026 version ups the amount of Beni Haruka paste to make the taste even more richly sweet, and every bite of the soft but dense cake is a moment of joy.

As is often the case with seasonal sweets in Japan, these are listed as being available while supplies last, so you’ll want to grab yours sooner rather than later.
